Writing

Books

A book is a set of ordinary notes read as one: chapters in an order, one title, one view of what is done and what is still a draft — and, when you want it, one document built from the lot. Every chapter stays a note like any other: it opens, links and previews as before, and Obsidian sees nothing it cannot read. The demo vault's Books/Signals is a small book to try things on, and its Guide/Books note, linked from Welcome, walks through it. (Not in 0.12.0.)

The master note

A book lives in a master note: one whose front matter says book: true and lists the chapters, in order, as links.

Books/Signals/Signals.md

---
book: true
title: "Signals: A Short Book"
numbering: per chapter
chapters:
  - "[[Senders and Receivers]]"
  - "[[Conventions]]"
  - "[[Deception]]"
---
  • It is the chapters: key that makes a note a master. A note that says book: true with no chapters: — notes about a book — is just a note.
  • numbering is per chapter, the default (Figure 2.3, Theorem 2.1, equation (2.1)), or continuous, straight through the book. Case and spacing in its value do not matter.
  • A chapter's title is its first # heading; failing that, the title in its front matter; failing that, its file name. Renaming a chapter's note renames it in the list too, as it does every other link to it, and a link's alias ([[Senders and Receivers|Ch. 1]]) survives every change the panel makes.
  • The master's own text is the book's prelude, before the first chapter — a dedication, an epigraph, or nothing — except an @bibliography (or @index) at its end, which goes after the last chapter: the book's one list of references.

The Book panel

A vault with a master has a Book tab in the right sidebar; a vault without one has no such tab. The command Book: show the Book panel opens it. It shows the book of the note you are in — the master or one of its chapters — or, from anywhere else, the book you opened last; a vault with several books has a list to pick from.

Each chapter is a row: its number, its title, its length in words, and its status. Under the list, the totals: 3 chapters · 368 words · 1 draft · 1 revised · 1 done.

  • Words are prose: front matter, code, maths and comments are not counted, so the status bar's count for the same note, which counts every word, is larger.
  • Status is the chapter's own status: property — draft, revised or done — set from the row's status chip. A chapter without one shows —, and the totals count it without a status.
  • Reorder by dragging a row by its grip, or focus a row and press ⌥↑ or ⌥↓.
  • × takes a chapter out of the book; its note stays where it is.
  • Add … puts the note you are in at the end of the book.
  • A chapter whose link finds no note is shown in red, with no such note.

Every change is an edit to a note — the master's chapters: list, or a chapter's status: — made the way you would make it yourself: an open editor takes it as an edit you can undo, and a note changed elsewhere at the same moment is held for you to resolve, as any conflict is. A master whose front matter Clew cannot rewrite safely (comments, unusual YAML) is shown but not changed.

Moving through a book

In a chapter, the status bar says where you are — Ch. 2 of Signals: A Short Book — and a click on it opens the Book panel. A note can be a chapter of two books: then the status bar names the one you opened or built most recently and adds · also in Course, and a click switches to the other.

Book: next chapter and Book: previous chapter step through the book of the note you are in. Neither has a key of its own; give them one in the hotkey editor.

Building a book

Build — the Book panel's PDF, LaTeX and HTML buttons, or File → Export → Book as PDF (via LaTeX), Book as LaTeX or Book as HTML — makes the whole book one document: the master's text, then each chapter in order, every chapter's front matter left out and its # heading made a chapter (a chapter with no # heading gets one from its title). Figures, theorems and equations are numbered as the master's numbering says, and a chapter's footnotes close that chapter, numbered from 1.

  • PDF and LaTeX go into a build/ folder beside the master, named after it — build/Signals.pdf, build/Signals.tex — and a rebuild replaces them. LaTeX's own files (.aux, .log, .bbl …) stay in build/ too, so nothing lands beside a chapter.
  • HTML is a small website in build/Signals/: index.html, the master's text with the contents; a page for each chapter, with previous, contents and next links; and references.html, linked from the contents, when the master ends with @bibliography. Clew opens index.html in your browser when the build is done. Each HTML build replaces the folder, the old one going to the Trash.
  • In a vault you have not trusted, a build runs no note code, as any export there does, and its pages are shown in Finder rather than opened, since they may carry the notes' own scripts; the notice says why.

A chapter link that finds no note stops the build, naming it. Whatever else the build had to say is listed under the panel's Last build: … · ⚠ 2, and each chapter's row carries its own ⚠ count. Each warning names its chapter and line — Deception:20 book: 2 level-1 headings in this chapter; each starts a chapter — and choosing it opens the chapter at that line.

What a chapter may set for itself

A book has one set of settings, the master's. A chapter's front matter may still add these for itself:

Bibliography
Joins the book's; a clash between two, or a chapter citing from another chapter's file, is warned.
Packages, LaTeX preamble
Join the book's one preamble; clashes are warned.
Lang or Language
That chapter's hyphenation and, in a book, its language's quotation marks.
Math macros
Added to the book's.
A <style>
Applies to that chapter's own page of an HTML build only.

Any other key a chapter sets is the master's to decide, and the build warns about it by name — unless the chapter sets it to the very value the book uses. That is why a chapter can keep Resolve citations: true for its own reading view without a warning, so long as the master says the same.

Not yet

Only chapters for now. Parts, and front and back matter, are not built yet: a master that lists parts, frontmatter or appendices is read without them, and the Book panel says so by name.
